title: Petra and the Visitor
premise: Quentin Eastwick, a meticulous pest controller whose notebooks are a form of prayer, is called to the hollow of Petra's Crossing where something leaves fingerprints on ceilings and doorframes. Waiting at the house is Wren, Quentin's childhood imaginary friend, unchanged after thirty years and no longer imaginary. As Quentin documents the escalating intrusions, they uncover that the town's founders bound a hungry presence beneath Petra's Crossing with an unfinished ritual, and that Wren was created by the founders' children to be its keeper — or its key. To save the town, Quentin must complete the ritual, but doing so means choosing between exposing the founders' crimes (the truth) and protecting the descendants who have become their found family; in the end Quentin finishes the rite by feeding it their own documented memories, unmaking Wren but leaving the truth written down for those who remain.
about_author: Juniper Sterling is the pen name of a former small-town archivist who spent years cataloguing property records, church ledgers, and unsent letters from towns that no longer exist. They write horror about paperwork, memory, and the things that wait patiently for people to come home.

chapters.title: Fingerprints on the Ceiling
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. Called to the Aldous house in Petra's Crossing, Quentin finds greasy handprints pressed into the plaster eleven feet up — too high for any ladder, too human for any animal. They document everything, as always, because documentation is a kind of prayer. The beat: professional calm stretched thin over genuine unease.

chapters.title: The Porch Light
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. At dusk, waiting on the porch steps, sits Wren — Quentin's childhood imaginary friend, unchanged at eight years old while Quentin is forty-one. Wren says only: 'You came back. It noticed.' The beat: vertigo of the past made flesh, tenderness curdling into dread.

chapters.title: What the Ledgers Say
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. In the county archive, Quentin cross-references the Aldous address with founding-era records and finds gaps — pages razored out, dates repeated, the same five family names signing everything. The beat: the thrill of research turning to the suspicion that someone curated the silence.

chapters.title: The Descendants
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. Quentin meets the five living descendants of the founders, summoned by anonymous letters none of them admit sending: Mara Aldous, the twins Oren and Odile Vetch, Pastor Ivo Crane, and young Tamsin, who claims she sees 'the tall one' too. The beat: strangers circling each other, already half a family.

chapters.title: Rules Wren Kept
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. Wren explains the old game's rules — don't answer if it knocks twice, count the fingers, never finish its sentences — and admits the rules were taught, not invented. The beat: childhood nostalgia revealed as training.

chapters.title: Something in the Walls
chapters.summary: POV Mara Aldous. Mara hears her dead mother's voice reciting inventory lists inside the walls and calls Quentin instead of the police. Together they find a crawlspace lined with children's drawings of a figure with too many joints. The beat: reluctant alliance, shared fear becoming trust.

chapters.title: The First Ritual
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. Deciphering the founders' ciphered ledger, Quentin learns the town was built over a 'hollow' and sealed by a ritual that requires five bloodlines and a keeper — and that it was left unfinished on purpose, renewed yearly by a payment no one will name. The beat: horror of inherited complicity.

chapters.title: Tamsin Counts the Fingers
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin. Ten-year-old Tamsin narrates her friendship with 'the tall one,' who asks her polite questions and grows more solid each time she answers. She tells Quentin because Wren told her to. The beat: innocence weaponized; the reader realizes answering is feeding it.

chapters.title: Odile's Confession
chapters.summary: POV Odile Vetch. Odile reveals the family secret: every generation, one descendant 'goes into the hollow' — officially emigrated, actually given. Her twin Oren vanished last autumn. The beat: grief and fury; loyalty to family versus the truth of what family has done.

chapters.title: What Wren Is For
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. Confronted, Wren admits the founders' children imagined a friend kind enough to take the payment in their place — and the hollow accepted the idea instead. Wren has been the substitute ever since, and the substitution is failing. The beat: heartbreak; the imaginary friend as sacrificial invention.

chapters.title: The Knocking
chapters.summary: POV Mara. It knocks twice at every house in Petra's Crossing on the same night. Those who answer are found smiling, wrong, reciting inventories. The town's denial cracks. The beat: communal dread; the horror stops being private.

chapters.title: Pastor Crane's Sermon
chapters.summary: POV Ivo Crane. The pastor, who has preached around the truth for decades, finally reads the founders' covenant aloud and is interrupted mid-sentence by his own congregation finishing it in unison. The beat: power's corruption — the ritual lives in the words people repeat without thinking.

chapters.title: Oren Comes Home
chapters.summary: POV Odile. Oren returns, physically intact, eyes wrong, speaking in the founders' cadences. He is gentle, helpful, and organizing the town toward 'completion.' The beat: the uncanny return; love for someone who may no longer be there.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Choice
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. The ledger's final page names the keeper's duty: when the substitute fails, the keeper completes the ritual by giving the hollow something true and irreplaceable. Quentin realizes why Wren waited thirty years on porches. The beat: dread of destiny; documentation as both shield and offering.

chapters.title: Burning the Notebooks
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. Someone burns Quentin's archive — twenty years of careful records — and Quentin discovers the ash arranged in fingerprints. Without documentation, Quentin's identity frays; the hollow is erasing the witness first. The beat: violation and despair; memory as contested territory.

chapters.title: Tamsin Is Asked
chapters.summary: POV Tamsin. The tall one asks Tamsin the final question — 'Will you come?' — and she almost answers yes, because it promised to bring Oren back whole. Wren intervenes, breaking a rule to do it, and begins to unravel. The beat: sacrifice; the protector spends itself.

chapters.title: Five Bloodlines
chapters.summary: POV Mara. The descendants gather in the founders' meetinghouse, each holding a relic of their line. Mara forces the vote: finish the ritual as the founders intended, with another payment, or find another way. The beat: found family forged under pressure; loyalty vs. truth made literal.

chapters.title: The Hollow Opens
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. At the sinkhole beneath the meetinghouse, the hollow rises — vast, patient, wearing the accumulated faces of everyone it was paid. Oren walks toward it willingly. The beat: awe and terror; the climax begins.

chapters.title: Finishing What Was Started
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. Quentin begins the completion rite but refuses the founders' terms, instead reading aloud twenty years of recovered memories — pages Tamsin secretly re-copied from memory — offering the hollow the one thing it cannot digest: being fully witnessed. The beat: defiance; prayer fulfilled through truth-telling.

chapters.title: Wren's Last Game
chapters.summary: POV Wren. Wren steps into the hollow as the final seal, choosing to end so the town doesn't have to feed it again, asking Quentin to remember them accurately — not kindly, accurately. The beat: devastating farewell; the imaginary friend becomes real by being mourned.

chapters.title: After the Crossing
chapters.summary: POV Mara. Weeks later: Oren wakes human but diminished, the town quietly reckons with its history, and the descendants keep meeting anyway — no longer obligated, choosing each other. The beat: bruised resolution; found family surviving the truth.

chapters.title: Documentation Is a Kind of Prayer
chapters.summary: POV Quentin. Quentin starts a new notebook, first entry a full account of Wren — every rule, every kindness, every lie — then closes it on the porch where Wren once waited. One set of small footprints appears in the frost, leading away. The beat: grief transmuted into record; an ending that honors both loss and survival.
